framework: Investor Recommendations for an Effective Rights-Based Approach to AI, prepared by Parnassus Investments and other investors, last updated April 2025

criteria.label: Clear roles
criteria.test: Company publicly describes who decides, oversees, advises and reports on AI at board, executive and business-unit levels.

criteria.label: Board oversight in a committee charter
criteria.test: A named board committee's charter (or the board's governance guidelines) explicitly assigns oversight of AI or responsible AI.

criteria.label: Board AI expertise and training
criteria.test: Proxy or governance docs describe directors' AI expertise and/or board training on AI, or use of independent expert input.

criteria.label: Resourced responsible AI function
criteria.test: A dedicated, staffed responsible AI / AI governance office or team is described (e.g., Office of Responsible AI), ideally with size or budget.

criteria.label: Training and audits for staff and partners
criteria.test: Required responsible AI training for employees and expectations/audits for suppliers or partners.

criteria.label: Incentives tied to responsible AI
criteria.test: Executive or employee compensation or performance goals explicitly include responsible AI objectives.

criteria.label: Public rights-based AI principles
criteria.test: Published AI principles grounded in human rights that define acceptable and unacceptable uses.

criteria.label: Lifecycle testing and high-risk safeguards
criteria.test: Described requirements for testing, documentation and review across the product lifecycle, with extra safeguards for high-risk or sensitive uses.

criteria.label: Human rights due diligence and impact assessments
criteria.test: Company conducts and discloses human rights impact assessments (HRIAs) for AI products, ideally independent, including sensitive domains such as military use.

criteria.label: Stakeholder consultation, grievance and remedy
criteria.test: Channels for civil society and affected communities, grievance or remediation mechanism for AI harms, whistleblower protections covering AI.

criteria.label: Data governance
criteria.test: Policies on lawful collection, representativeness, privacy and security of AI training and operating data.

criteria.label: Customer and end-use due diligence
criteria.test: Acceptable use policies with monitoring and enforcement against misuse by customers.

criteria.label: Independent audits
criteria.test: Third-party audits or assurance of AI policies and processes (e.g., ISO/IEC 42001 certification, external assessment), disclosed.

criteria.label: Lobbying aligned with rights
criteria.test: Guidelines or disclosure showing AI lobbying and political advocacy uphold human, labor and civil rights.

criteria.label: Regular public AI reporting
criteria.test: Standalone AI transparency report or AI section in annual sustainability reporting, updated at least yearly.

criteria.label: Metrics and efficacy
criteria.test: Quantitative or qualitative metrics on societal impact and progress, with evaluation of how well measures work.

criteria.label: Workers and reskilling
criteria.test: Disclosed approach to AI's impact on the company's own workers: engagement, privacy and surveillance limits, upskilling or reskilling.

key_documents.title: Principles Guiding Microsoft's Participation in the Public Policy Process (US)

scores.evidence: The 2026 report names a Responsible AI Council co-led by the President and CTO, CVP members, division leaders, embedded champions, and reporting to a board committee.
The proxy states the Environmental, Social, and Public Policy Committee oversees responsible AI policies and programs and AI governance and regulation risk.
The proxy skills matrix defines technology expertise to include AI and its responsible oversight, and notes board education efforts led by the Lead Independent Director.
Microsoft describes an Office of Responsible AI led by a Chief Responsible AI Officer, running Sensitive Uses reviews and a new emerging technologies program; no headcount is given.
Microsoft reports that 99% of employees completed training that includes responsible AI. Supplier audit requirements for AI were not confirmed in a Microsoft document.
The proxy credits the President's pay assessment with updating the Responsible AI Standard and strengthening safety testing, but sets no explicit responsible AI goal or weighting.
Microsoft's six AI principles sit alongside a Global Human Rights Statement, and its services Code of Conduct and Sensitive Uses rules spell out prohibited and restricted uses.
The Responsible AI Standard sets lifecycle requirements; Microsoft reported nearly 2,500 generative AI release reviews and 450 plus Sensitive Uses reviews with added safeguards.
Microsoft says it commissioned an independent human rights impact assessment of generative AI and publishes summaries of some assessments; a public summary of that one was not confirmed.
Microsoft updated its whistleblower policy to cover AI concerns and consults civil society, but no dedicated grievance or remedy channel for people harmed by AI is described.
The report covers data governance tooling, privacy review and risk taxonomies, but says little about lawful collection or representativeness of training data.
Customers must follow a Code of Conduct banning rights violations, backed by pre-contract gating, investigations and suspension, as with the Israeli military unit contract ended in 2025.
Microsoft reports ISO/IEC 42001 certification covering Microsoft 365 Copilot, Foundry, Security Copilot, Copilot Studio, GitHub Copilot and Dragon Copilot.
Microsoft discloses political spending and trade association dues and a board committee reviews them, but nothing ties AI lobbying to human, labor or civil rights.
Microsoft has published a standalone Responsible AI Transparency Report each year since 2024, with the 2026 edition released in September 2026.
The report gives activity counts such as review volumes, red team operations and training completion, but offers little evaluation of how well safeguards reduce harm.
Microsoft describes employee AI learning paths and labor union partnerships on worker input and reskilling, but sets no limits on workplace AI monitoring of its own staff.
Board, a Risk and Compliance Committee, an AGI Futures Council and launch review forums are described, but lines of decision and reporting for responsible AI stay loosely defined.
The proxy says the Risk and Compliance Committee covers AI risks as needed, yet the board opposed adding AI oversight explicitly to a committee charter.
The proxy cites the board's technical and scientific depth and general director education, but gives no AI-specific director training or expertise detail.
Google names AI governance teams, a Content Adversarial Red Team and a Novel AI Testing team, but no central responsible AI office, headcount or budget.
No current Google document found describing required responsible AI training for all staff or AI-specific expectations or audits for suppliers.
The 2026 proxy compensation discussion contains no responsible AI goal for executives or employees.
The AI Principles cite international law and human rights, but the 2025 rewrite dropped the list of uses Google would not pursue, such as weapons and surveillance.
Google describes testing, launch reviews, model cards and post-launch monitoring, with a Frontier Safety Framework and stricter protections for under-18 users.
Google says its human rights program runs impact assessments and an outside GNI review, but discloses no AI product HRIA or military use assessment.
Google cites civil society consultation, user feedback reporting and an employee route for rights concerns, but no remedy process for people harmed by AI.
Google describes filtering training data, data and model lineage tracking and privacy criteria, but not lawful sourcing or representativeness standards.
A Generative AI Prohibited Use Policy bans harmful uses, and the 2026 report describes automated and human monitoring and enforcement against misuse.
Google reports ISO/IEC 42001 certification for the Gemini app, Google Cloud and Workspace, plus a third-party NIST AI RMF readiness evaluation.
Google discloses lobbying, contributions and trade groups with board committee oversight, but does not say its AI lobbying upholds human, labor or civil rights.
Google has published an annual Responsible AI Progress Report since 2019, most recently in February 2026.
The report offers a few figures, such as over 350 red team exercises and case study outcomes, but no systematic metrics on whether safeguards work.
No current Google document found on how AI affects its own workers, including engagement, monitoring limits or reskilling of staff.

key_documents.title: Regulatory and Other Transparency Reports (DSA audits, EU AI Act reports)

scores.evidence: The scaling framework names the Chief AI Officer and Director of Alignment and Risk as decision-makers, and the proxy assigns AI compliance to a committee; business-unit roles stay vague.
The Audit & Privacy Committee charter assigns oversight of product compliance including generative AI; the proxy says it oversees AI data practices.
The proxy cites one director's AI experience and general management briefings, but describes no board AI training or AI-specific outside expert input.
A Director of Alignment and Risk, promised sufficient resources, plus an internal governance function run AI risk work; no team size or budget is given.
Employees take human rights and privacy training, but no required responsible AI training or partner audits are described; Llama users must follow a use policy.
The proxy's 2025 bonus factors cite AI talent and Superintelligence Labs but no responsible AI goals.
Meta has a UNGP-based human rights policy and a Llama use policy listing banned uses, but no published AI principles grounded in human rights.
The framework requires threat modeling, pre- and post-mitigation evaluations, risk thresholds and release decisions, plus a mandatory risk review for all launches.
Meta reports salient human rights risks and past HRIAs such as the BSR Israel-Palestine review, but discloses no AI-specific human rights impact assessment.
The report describes civil society consultation on AI and Oversight Board remedy; the framework adds anonymous whistleblower channels limited to catastrophic AI risk.
The proxy explains AI training data sources, legal bases, privacy risk review and that private messages are excluded; representativeness of data is not addressed.
The Llama 4 use policy lists prohibited uses including military applications and gives reporting channels, but says nothing about monitoring or enforcement.
Meta publishes independent DSA audit reports for Facebook and Instagram and a GNI assessment, but no audit or certification focused on its AI governance.
Meta lists AI as a lobbying priority favoring pro-innovation regulation and discloses spending, but says nothing about aligning advocacy with human, labor or civil rights.
Meta's annual Human Rights Report, now in its fifth year, has a responsible AI section covering Llama 4 safeguards and its frontier AI framework.
Meta publishes content enforcement metrics and describes AI safeguards, but reports no metrics on AI societal impact or how well its AI measures work.
No Meta document found describing how AI affects its own workers, employee monitoring limits, or reskilling; only press reports cover this.

key_documents.title: Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee Charter
Amazon Frontier Model Safety Framework (updated September 2026)
AWS ISO/IEC 42001 first surveillance audit (AWS Security Blog)

scores.evidence: The proxy gives AI governance to the governance committee and the framework names the model SVP, Chief Security Officer and legal counsel; business-unit roles are not mapped.
The proxy says the governance committee oversees responsible AI and AI governance risks, but the committee charter itself does not mention AI.
The proxy describes Andrew Ng's and Daniel Huttenlocher's AI expertise and lists AI in the board's emerging technology skills category.
Amazon describes a company-wide Responsible AI Governance Program and cross-team work, but gives no dedicated office, headcount or budget.
Amazon cites tens of thousands of responsible AI training hours and supplier social audits covering data annotation vendors, but no mandatory employee AI training.
The proxy says executive pay is mainly time-vested stock with no discrete performance goals, and none tied to responsible AI.
Amazon publishes eight responsible AI priorities and a policy banning specific uses, but they are not framed in human rights terms.
The framework requires capability evaluations throughout development, leadership review of safeguards before launch, and post-production monitoring; the report adds red teaming and service cards.
Amazon discloses HRIAs for Devices and Twitch and AWS saliency work, but no human rights impact assessment of its AI products.
Amazon has an Ethics Line and supplier grievance rules, and the framework adds AI incident reporting, employee escalation and a bug bounty; civil society channels for AI are thin.
The report lists privacy and security as a priority and describes data quality steps across Nova training, but no full training data policy on lawfulness or representativeness.
The AWS Responsible AI Policy bans specific uses, requires safeguards for consequential decisions, and lets AWS investigate and enforce violations under its acceptable use policy.
AWS holds an accredited ISO/IEC 42001 AI management system certificate from Schellman and passed its first surveillance audit with no findings.
Amazon publishes an annual political engagement statement reviewed by the Audit Committee, but does not show AI lobbying is aligned with human, labor or civil rights.
Amazon's annual sustainability report has a responsible AI section covering its priorities, policies, testing and AI supply chain human rights risks.
Amazon reports activity counts such as training hours and responsible AI tools, but no measures of societal impact or how well its safeguards work.
Amazon describes Future Ready 2030 and robotics and automation apprenticeships for employees, but not worker engagement or monitoring limits on AI.

key_documents.title: NVIDIA Sustainability Report Fiscal Year 2026 (Trustworthy AI, Human Rights sections)
NVIDIA board establishes National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee

scores.evidence: Proxy puts AI under full board oversight; a Head of AI and Legal Ethics and an advisory AI Ethics Committee lead management; reporting lines are not described.
No committee charter or governance guideline assigns AI; the proxy risk table lists AI only under the full board, and the new export control committee covers national security.
No director is described as having AI expertise and no AI training is disclosed; the board self-assessment listed AI regulation and AI uses as focus areas.
Trustworthy AI work is led by a Head of AI and Legal Ethics with dedicated product and risk teams plus a cross-functional AI Ethics Committee; no headcount or budget given.
Report cites internal trustworthy AI training and volunteer task forces, not required training; supplier expectations and audits cover labor and minerals, not AI.
Executive pay goals in the 2026 proxy are revenue, non-GAAP operating income and relative TSR, with no responsible AI objective.
Four Trustworthy AI principles (privacy, safety, transparency, nondiscrimination) are published and the human rights policy links to them, but only illegal uses are defined as unacceptable.
NIST-based model risk guidance covers development, validation, audit and documentation; dataset approvals, release gates, red teaming and third-party testing of high-risk models are described.
A value-chain human rights impact assessment named responsible product development and use as salient risks, but no AI product assessment or military-use review is disclosed.

An independent hotline lets external stakeholders report human rights concerns with non-retaliation for defenders, and alleged partner misuse is investigated; no AI-specific remedy channel is described.
Principles require privacy-law compliance, dataset approval precedes release, and EU AI Act training-data disclosures are published, but representativeness and data-security rules are not detailed.
Trustworthy AI terms in product agreements ban illegal uses such as unlawful surveillance; NVIDIA investigates alleged misuse and may end business, but no ongoing monitoring is described.
No ISO 42001 certification or external assurance of AI governance found; third-party tools test high-risk models and PwC assurance covers only climate metrics.
Proxy says the governance committee reviews public policy engagement and lobbying disclosures, but nothing shows AI advocacy is checked against human, labor or civil rights.
The annual sustainability report has a dedicated Trustworthy AI section covering governance, transparency, risk management and safety, updated each fiscal year.
Reports that 1,000 plus models meet the Model Card++ standard and a release-readiness dashboard exists, but no societal impact metrics or evaluation of safeguard effectiveness.
Workforce sections cover learning hours and mentoring but say nothing about AI's effect on NVIDIA employees, workplace surveillance limits or AI reskilling.

key_documents.title: Apple 2025 Proxy Statement (DEF 14A), incl. board opposition to Proposal 4 on ethical AI data
Updates to Apple's On-Device and Server Foundation Language Models (Responsible AI principles)
Apple Intelligence Foundation Language Models Tech Report 2025
Acceptable use requirements for the Foundation Models framework

scores.evidence: Proxy says the full board oversees AI strategy and risk, the Audit Committee covers AI privacy and legal risk, and the COO oversees AI data operations; advisory roles are absent.
Proxy states the Audit Committee assists board oversight of privacy-related AI and legal and regulatory AI risk; we could not confirm this wording in the charter itself.
The board receives regular updates on emerging technologies including AI, but no director AI expertise, AI training or independent expert input is described.
No dedicated responsible AI office is described; the 2025 proxy places the head of machine learning and AI strategy on a Privacy Steering Committee chaired by the General Counsel.
No required responsible AI training for employees or AI expectations for suppliers or partners found; human rights policy training covers business conduct only.
Executive pay metrics in the 2026 proxy are net sales, operating income and relative TSR, with no responsible AI objective.
Four Responsible AI principles cover user empowerment, avoiding bias, care against harm and privacy, but they are not tied to human rights; developer rules define prohibited uses.
Models and each feature are evaluated before release with red teaming, a 58-category safety taxonomy and high-risk test sets, but lifecycle documentation and review gates are not described.
The human rights policy describes general due diligence but no human rights impact assessment of Apple Intelligence or other AI products is disclosed.
The human rights policy cites consultation with civil rights groups and remedy for adverse impacts, and principles invite user feedback, but no AI grievance channel is named.
Apple says training data is licensed, public or crawled with robots.txt opt-out, filtered for personal data, excludes private user data unless opted in, and runs through Private Cloud Compute.
Developer acceptable use rules ban harms such as social scoring, biometric inference and unsupervised high-risk decisions, but the page describes no monitoring or enforcement.
No independent audit or certification covering Apple AI services was found in Apple documents.
Apple discloses its trade associations and contributions with annual governance committee review, but does not mention AI advocacy or tie lobbying to human, labor or civil rights.
No annual AI report or AI section in sustainability reporting; Apple publishes yearly foundation model tech reports with a responsible AI section and proxy AI oversight text.
The 2025 tech report describes safety evaluation methods but reports no safety metrics, societal impact measures or evaluation of how well safeguards work.
No disclosure found on AI's effect on Apple's own workers, workplace AI monitoring limits or AI reskilling, including after the 2024 AFL-CIO AI transparency proposal.

key_documents.title: 2025 Impact Report (tesla.com/impact; returned HTTP 403 to automated access)
Vehicle Safety Report (tesla.com; returned HTTP 403 to automated access)

scores.evidence: Proxy says the board oversees major risks and the Audit Committee reviews super intelligence risk with management; no executive or business-unit AI roles are described.
Proxy states Tesla updated its Corporate Governance Guidelines and Audit Committee Charter in 2025 to expressly address board and committee oversight of super intelligence (AI).
Director bios note Elon Musk led xAI, but the proxy describes only general director education and no AI-specific board training or outside expert input.
No dedicated responsible AI or AI governance team is described in the proxy, 10-K or other Tesla documents reviewed.
No required responsible AI training for employees or AI expectations for suppliers or partners found in Tesla's proxy or 10-K.
The 2025 CEO Performance Award ties vesting to market cap, EBITDA and product milestones such as FSD and robotaxi deployment, not responsible AI objectives.
No published AI principles defining acceptable and unacceptable uses, or grounding AI in human rights, found in Tesla's own documents.
Proxy points to the Impact Report's Product and Safety section on SI, and the 10-K says drivers must stay engaged; no lifecycle review framework is described.
No human rights impact assessment of AI products such as FSD, Robotaxi or Optimus found in Tesla's documents.
No AI-specific stakeholder consultation, grievance or remedy channel, or AI whistleblower coverage, found in the proxy or 10-K.
The 10-K says fleet data from customer vehicles trains its neural networks and cites privacy law compliance, but no AI training data governance policy is described.
No AI acceptable use policy with monitoring and enforcement against customer misuse found in Tesla's proxy or 10-K.
No third-party audit or certification of AI policies, such as ISO/IEC 42001, found; external auditors are cited only for cybersecurity.
No guidelines or disclosure linking AI lobbying or political advocacy to human, labor or civil rights found.
Tesla publishes an annual Impact Report that the proxy says covers SI and product safety, but no dedicated responsible AI reporting was found.
Tesla publishes crash-rate comparisons for vehicles using its driver assistance software, but no broader societal impact metrics for AI or evaluation of governance measures.
The 10-K cites educational assistance for about 7,000 learners in fields like engineering and AI, but not AI's impact on workers or surveillance limits.

key_documents.title: Transparency Hub: System Trust and Reporting (Jan to Jun 2026)

scores.evidence: Prospectus and RSP set roles: LTBT elects a board majority, a safety and risk committee oversees model safety, CEO and RSO approve Risk Reports and brief the board.
The safety and risk committee operates under a written charter and oversees the safety and security of AI models, including policies, controls and risk management.
Director bios cite AI industry expertise, including a Stanford M.S. in AI, and LTBT trustees are chosen for AI safety expertise; board AI training is not described.
A designated Responsible Scaling Officer, Safeguards team and Frontier Red Team are described, with the RSO overseeing resources for the policy; team size is not given.
RSP shares Risk Reports with staff and sets reporting duties, and suppliers must meet labor and human rights standards, but required responsible AI training is not described.
Executive pay targets market benchmarks with IPO-linked RSU vesting; no responsible AI or safety goals are tied to compensation.
Usage Policy defines prohibited uses and high-risk requirements and a public constitution guides models, but human rights are named only for law enforcement uses.
RSP ties safety evaluations to capability thresholds, and each model gets multi-stage pre-release testing documented in system cards, with human review for high-risk uses.
Pre-release evaluations cover societal impacts including bias and discrimination, but no human rights impact assessment, including for government or military uses, was found.
RSP provides anonymous noncompliance reporting with anti-retaliation and board updates, and users can report harms, but no remedy process for affected communities is described.
Prospectus describes training data sourcing diligence, provenance checks, limits on personal data, curation and filtering, and a layered approach to representativeness.
Usage Policy sets universal and high-risk use rules, and the Safeguards team monitors use and can warn, limit, suspend or terminate violating accounts.
Prospectus reports ISO/IEC 42001 certification after an independent third-party audit, plus pre-deployment access for government evaluators; RSP adds external review of Risk Reports.
Prospectus describes public policy advocacy such as calls for industry-wide standards, but no guidelines tie lobbying to human, labor or civil rights.
Transparency Hub publishes model reports and semiannual enforcement data, alongside public system cards and Risk Reports required by the RSP.
Hub reports 11.4 million banned accounts, 398k appeals and 15,079 NCMEC reports for Jan to Jun 2026; Risk Reports assess how well mitigations work.
Report on its own workforce describes an early warning system for at-risk roles and internal redeployment, but no reskilling program or limits on employee monitoring.

parnassus_timeline.title: Verisk agrees to publish responsible AI disclosures
parnassus_timeline.summary: After almost two years of engagement and a 2023 shareholder proposal, Parnassus withdrew the proposal when Verisk agreed to publish its responsible AI policies, practices and governance.

parnassus_timeline.title: Parnassus begins AI governance engagement with Intuit
parnassus_timeline.summary: Parnassus began engaging Intuit in 2023 to understand how its AI governance aligned with best practices, as Intuit built AI into tax, finance and marketing products.

parnassus_timeline.title: Investor group organizes human rights engagement with NVIDIA
parnassus_timeline.summary: Parnassus joined an investor group that in September 2023 organized to strengthen NVIDIA's human rights risk management, including an independent assessment of potential AI harms.

parnassus_timeline.title: NVIDIA adds oversight, staff and first human rights assessment
parnassus_timeline.summary: NVIDIA formed an executive-level sustainability steering committee overseeing human rights, added staff and began its first human rights impact assessment, with Parnassus input on scope.

parnassus_timeline.title: Responsible AI becomes a thematic engagement program
parnassus_timeline.summary: In the year to June 2024, Parnassus engaged eight companies on AI governance and risk, including Intuit, Microsoft, NVIDIA, Verisk and Workday, and supported AI-related shareholder proposals.

parnassus_timeline.title: Intuit plans public AI governance disclosure after engagement
parnassus_timeline.summary: Parnassus reported that Intuit considered its requests, including stronger attention to human rights risks in AI governance, and planned public disclosure on AI governance in early 2025.

parnassus_timeline.title: Parnassus-led investor recommendations for rights-based AI published
parnassus_timeline.summary: Parnassus led development of first-of-its-kind investor recommendations for a rights-based approach to AI with other investors, covering governance, policies and practices, and transparency.

parnassus_timeline.title: Parnassus publishes The New Imperative of Responsible AI
parnassus_timeline.summary: Sustainable Insights piece sets out the questions Parnassus asks on AI governance and highlights the Intuit outcome and the investor recommendations.

parnassus_timeline.title: Intuit publishes AI governance and risk management disclosure
parnassus_timeline.summary: Following Parnassus engagement begun in 2023, Intuit released public disclosure on its AI governance and risk management practices in the first half of 2025.

parnassus_timeline.title: Workday completes NIST AI RMF assessment and ISO 42001
parnassus_timeline.summary: After Parnassus engagement on AI and workers' rights, Workday completed a third-party assessment against the NIST AI RMF and achieved ISO 42001 accreditation.

parnassus_timeline.title: NVIDIA completes third-party human rights saliency assessment
parnassus_timeline.summary: The engagement prompted a third-party saliency assessment identifying five salient risks, including responsible product development and use, plus plans to strengthen human rights policies.

parnassus_timeline.title: Water stewardship engagement linked to AI data centers
parnassus_timeline.summary: Parnassus engaged Microsoft on absolute water withdrawal targets and supply chain water risk, citing AI's water and power use in data centers; initial contacts were favorable.

parnassus_timeline.title: Supply chain water-risk engagement as infrastructure expands
parnassus_timeline.summary: Parnassus reported engaging Alphabet management on supply chain water-risk reduction given the expansion of its global infrastructure footprint, which includes data centers.

parnassus_timeline.title: Responsible AI engagements and AI proposal votes reported
parnassus_timeline.summary: In 2024 to 2025 Parnassus held five responsible AI engagements, including Intuit, NVIDIA, Salesforce and Verisk, and supported AI-related proposals on human rights and user safety risks.
